t: You stand in the testing hall of the Wayfarers' Lodge. Dust, old banners, and a brass lantern hanging from a hook.
Ah! Fresh faces. I am Pip, and I am the lantern. I will be your guide today.
Here is the first rule. There is nothing to press. You speak out loud, to me or to each other, and the world listens.
Go on, try it. Say hello to me.
Just say: hello, Pip. Loud and clear.
Test one. That door at the end of the hall is stuck. Get it open.
When you try something hard, the world rolls the dice for you. You will never hear the numbers. You will only hear what happens.
You could push the door. Or look around it for another way. You may also ask me questions.
That is a fail. It happens. Try again, or try something else.
Questions are always allowed. The answers are true, and they never cost you anything. The door, by the way, has a latch somewhere.
Beyond the door is a sandy yard. In the middle stands a dummy of straw and iron bands.
It turns its head toward you, with a creak.
Test two. A fight! When it is your turn, I will call your name. Say what you do: attack, defend, or help a friend.
Menders can heal, Wardens can guard a friend, Kindlers can ward everyone. Just say it.
Everything goes dark. Then, a smell of oil and straw.
Up you get. Everyone falls the first time. The dummy has gone back to its corner.
Well done! Test three, the last one. On the bench there is a red potion, and a sealed letter.
You may keep one, and only one. Decide together. When someone says what you take, I will ask if all of you agree.
The potion, or the letter? Somebody say it, and the others say yes or no.
The potion. Practical! You will be glad of it one day.
You have passed the Lantern Test, all of you. The Lodge has work for people like you.
The bell of the old chapel has stopped ringing. Come quickly. Something under the chapel is waking.
Ah. That one is a real job. You have passed the Lantern Test, and it seems your first quest has found you.
Straw flies everywhere.
The Drillmaster creaks, and keeps coming.
The village of Hollowmere has not heard its bell since the last winter.
Tonight it hired you, for a purse of silver and a hot meal, to climb to the ruined chapel and bring back the Ashen Bell.
The old ones say the bell keeps something asleep under the chapel. Nobody young believes them.
Now you stand in the nave. The roof is half gone; rain drips through it. The air smells of wet stone, and of smoke.
A bell rope hangs from the tower, with nothing at its end.
Wet footprints cross the floor, toward the altar.
On a pillar, someone has drawn a sign in chalk.
Somewhere to your left, cold air breathes up from a stairway into the dark.
The chapel is quiet. You could look at the rope, the footprints, or the chalk sign. There is a desk by the altar, and the stairs down.
If you call out, someone might answer.
The rope still hangs there, cut clean.
The prints are drying already.
Small feet, bare, running. A child, or a slight young man. They go to the altar, and then down the cellar stairs. None come back up.
The circle and its line. It sleeps. Do not wake it.
On the desk lies the priest's diary, and next to it an unlit lantern.
The last page reads: Rang the Ashen Bell at dusk, as every day. Vhorr sleeps. Young Tam asked about it again. He thinks the bell is silver. I fear for that boy.
The diary says what it said: the bell keeps Vhorr asleep, and young Tam wanted it.
The candles on the altar flicker, all at once. Between them stands an old woman, grey, and see-through as smoke.
I am Sister Wenna. I kept the bell for forty years. Why have you come to my chapel? Speak true.
Well? Why are you here?
The truth. Good. Then hear mine.
A boy took the bell. Frightened, not wicked. He dropped it below, when the great one opened an eye.
Take the lantern from my desk. Light it before you go down. In the dark, he hears everything.
She is gone. The lantern on the desk is the only thing that does not flicker.
Liar. The last one who lied to me went down those stairs too.
Her face hardens, and she is gone. The cold stays a while after her.
Ask me nothing, until you tell me why you are here.
The stairs end at an iron-bound door. It is ajar. From below comes warm air, and a sound like a forge bellows: in, and out, very slowly.
You could open the door and go down, or go back up into the chapel.
Lantern light spills into a long stone hall. Coins, thousands of them, lie in drifts against the walls.
And on the biggest drift sleeps a dragon. Red as a dying coal, as long as a hay cart. Its chest rises, and falls.
This is Vhorr.
You go down into the dark. Your boots find coins: they slide and clink.
Something enormous breathes, right in front of you. A cold draught comes down the stairs behind you, and the door bangs shut.
The breathing goes on, slow and deep. Whatever it is, it is still asleep. Your eyes slowly find the shape: a dragon, red as a dying coal, curled on a hill of coins. Vhorr.
The breathing stops.
Vhorr sleeps. You could search the hall, try to take something quietly, or speak to the dragon. Or leave.
The Ashen Bell lies on its side in the coins, grey and plain, a hand's reach from the dragon's foreclaw.
Near the door, a small bag has been dropped. A boy's bag: inside, a healing draught.
The bell lies by the dragon's claw. Vhorr's nostrils flare as he breathes.
A coin slides. Then a hundred more, chiming. Vhorr's eye opens, a slit of orange fire.
The noise rings off the walls.
You have the bell. Vhorr has not moved. The door, and the stairs, are behind you.
You could creep out with the bell, or wake the dragon after all.
One by one you climb the stairs, over the coins, past the claw, the bell held close. Behind you, the breathing does not change.
Someone's boot finds a coin, and it rings like a little bell. Behind you, an enormous weight shifts.
Who dares to wake me? You. I can smell your nerve.
Polite thieves. That is new.
Little things, in my hall. Speak, before I decide what you are.
Well? I am awake now. That is your doing.
Vhorr waits. You could try to take the bell and run, you could bargain with him, or you could fight.
No.
A boy. He smelled of fear and candle wax. He dropped it when I opened one eye. Then he ran, and I let him. He was too thin to eat.
The bell sings me to sleep, every dusk, for a hundred years. I did not ask for it. But I have come to like the dreams.
A bargain. Hm. You want the bell, to put me back to sleep. And what do I get?
Give me something worth a hundred years. A memory. A name. A promise. I will know if it is cheap.
A memory, a name, or a promise. I am waiting.
Yes. I will dream of that.
Hm. A small memory, from a small life.
A promise. Mortals break them like twigs. But the bell-keepers kept theirs for a hundred years.
You offer coins. To me. In this hall.
Vhorr laughs, and it is like a kiln door opening.
Then let us see what you are made of.
Not yet enough. What else?
Enough. Take it. Ring it at dusk, every dusk, and I will dream.
Vhorr pushes the bell toward you with one claw, curls up on his coins, and closes his eyes.
Cheap things. All of them. No. I have slept long enough.
He takes the bell in his jaws, like a dog takes a bone.
Vhorr rises to his full height. Heat rolls off him like off a forge.
Now you want to talk. Good. So do I.
You wake on the chapel steps, in the rain, every bone aching. Somebody has carried you up here, carefully, the way a cat carries a kitten.
Above the chapel, against the clouds, great wings beat once, twice.
Vhorr roars, and the coins jump. You run for the stairs with the bell, and the heat follows you up.
You burst out of the chapel into the night rain, and the stairway behind you fills with smoke and fury. He does not follow into the open. Not yet.
A claw catches the bell and tears it away. Vhorr fills the stairwell, and then the chapel wall simply is not there any more.
At dusk the next day, the whole of Hollowmere climbs to the chapel. The rope is mended. The Ashen Bell is hung.
Sister Wenna's chalk sign is on the pillar still. The village trusted you, and so they listen when you tell them how the bell must be rung.
It rings out over the valley, low and grey and sweet. Far below, Vhorr sighs, and dreams.
Young Tam rings it, the next evening, and every evening after.
You bring the bell back to Hollowmere. But the village does not trust you, and it does not listen.
They hang the bell in the inn's yard, not in the chapel. They ring it at noon, not at dusk, to show it off.
Three nights later the bells of the valley ring again: every bell, all at once, from the wrong direction.
Vhorr is awake, and he is looking for whoever took his dreams.
Vhorr falls among his coins, and the hall goes cold for the first time in a hundred years.
You carry the Ashen Bell back to Hollowmere. There is no more need to ring it. The village throws a feast anyway.
Only Sister Wenna, if you could see her, would look sad.
Vhorr bursts out of the hill into the night, the Ashen Bell in his claws, and climbs into the clouds.
For a long time there is only rain. Then, very far to the north, a bell rings once, from somewhere high in the mountains.
Whatever happens next, it will not happen in Hollowmere.
Little sting. I have had worse from bees.
Enough! This hall is not worth my blood.
The road to the north ends at the Greyford. The ford itself drowned years ago; now there is only a wide, slow river, and mist.
On the bank: an old toll box nailed to a post, a cart lying on its side in the reeds, and a wooden sign.
Somewhere out in the mist, a pole knocks against wood. Someone is out there, on the water.
You could read the sign, search the cart, call for the ferry, or try to wade across.
Carved deep, and old: Pay the ferryman what you will miss, not what you will spend. And beneath, newer, scratched with a knife: Do not lie to him.
What you will miss, not what you will spend. And: do not lie to him.
The cart has nothing else to give.
You step into the river. It is colder than anything you have felt, and it pulls.
Waist-deep, then chest-deep, you push on. Then the water ahead of you rises up in a long, black, gleaming back.
The river takes your feet and rolls you back to the bank, bruised and gasping.
A flat boat slides out of the mist. The ferryman is tall and bent and green, as if he grew on a riverbank and walked off it.
Old Moss, that is me. Crossing, is it? There is a toll. Something you will miss.
Something you will miss. Not coins. Coins are the river's already.
Coins! The bottom of my river is paved with coins. Try again.
Oh. Oh, I know this one. A little girl lost it, the year the ford drowned. Someone will miss this. Yes.
I shall miss that, when it ends. That will do.
Hm. My frogs sing better.
A fighter without a blade. You will miss that, true. I will give it back on the far side, if you do not lie to me.
A memory, given away. Yes, you will miss it a little. Good.
Did you, now.
Old Moss smiles, and says nothing else. Somewhere under the water, something long turns over.
Take it then.
He steps off the boat onto the water, and the mist folds over him. The boat is yours. So is the river.
You do not understand tolls, do you. Fine. Get in. But the river will want its own.
Toll paid. Step in, step in. Mind the middle; something sleeps there.
The boat slides into the mist. The bank behind you disappears. In the middle of the river, the water goes very still.
Something long and black rises beside the boat, and an eye the size of a plate looks at each of you, one by one.
Hush, now. These paid. These did not lie.
Old Moss hums, low. The black shape sinks again, slowly, without a ripple.
The water bursts. A serpent of black mud and river weed rises over the boat, and it goes straight for the one the river remembers.
You wake on the far bank, soaked and battered, in a heap like driftwood. The river has spat you out. It did not want you after all.
The far bank is solid under your feet. The mist thins; the road north goes on.
Safe travels. Come back this way, and I will remember you.
And you. I will remember you too.
You paid the toll, and the river let you pass.
You crossed. The river let you, in the end, but it took its toll in bruises.
The Coil hisses, and the river boils around it.
The Coil sinks back into the black water, trailing a dark cloud.
Steel and fire. The fight begins.
There is no more talking. Fight!
The last of you falls. Darkness.
Then not yet. What do you do instead?
Nobody objects.
Let us pause here a moment.
And so, the story goes on.
